<reason>Side A (CON) wins by exposing a fatal contradiction in the proposition’s case. While Side B (PRO) makes a strong arithmetic argument about land scarcity, Side A decisively shows that transitioning to composting/alkaline hydrolysis immediately excludes working-class Muslim and Orthodox Jewish families whose faiths mandate intact earth burial—a mandate Side B admits is "non-negotiable" [B4.3] yet claims their scattering gardens satisfy [B5.2]. Side A effectively weaponizes this concession, framing the proposition as "immediate religious exclusion" versus Side B’s "deferred eviction" via satellite cemeteries. Side A also lands a clean hit on Side B’s internal contradiction: criticizing green burial for "locking up acreage" while promising the same land stays green as "memorial forests." Side B’s response—that physics makes permanent plots impossible—fails to explain how their plan actually accommodates these faiths, merely asserting that the alternative is also finite. Side A’s alternative (green burial, multi-layered plots, eventual satellite cemeteries) is more nuanced and directly addresses the proposition’s false dichotomy, whereas Side B’s case relies on a tragic-choice framing that doesn’t resolve the immediate justice violation.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A’s Rebuttal 2 (Turn 8) and Closing (Turn 10) form the decisive exchange: A seizes on B’s concession in [B4.3] that intact burial is non-negotiable for Orthodox Jews and Muslims, then exposes the contradiction with B’s later claim in [B5.2] that compost groves leave cemeteries "accessible to all faiths." A frames this as a "locked gate" for these communities, turning B’s own words into evidence of state-mandated exclusion. This pressure was not adequately answered by B, leaving A with the cleaner path to victory on the religious pluralism and immediate justice clash.</best_rebuttal>
